title: Otitis Media (Acute)
summary:
- This covers acute otitis media-for management of other indications including chronic suppurative otitis media, otitis media with effusion (glue ear) and recurrent acute otitis media, CKS is a useful reference.
- Do not issue a prescription for an antimicrobial to a patient who is likely to have a self-limiting condition.
- Acute otitis media is a self-limiting infection. It mainly affects children and can be viral or bacterial in origin. Symptoms can last up to 1 week, although most people get better within 3 days without antibiotics regardless of the cause (bacteria or virus).  Advise patients regarding self-care, patient self-care information is available here and patient information leaflet available here.
- Treatment options include no antibiotic prescription, a back-up antibiotic prescription or an immediate antibiotic prescription. Refer to NICE visual summary for full details and to aid decision making.

- Groups who may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics:

  -     Children and young people with acute otitis media and otorrhoea
  -     Children under 2 years with acute otitis media in both ears

- An immediate antibiotic prescription should be offered if the child or young person is systemically very unwell or has symptoms and signs of a more serious illness or has a high risk of complications. Refer to hospital if severe systemic infection or complications like mastoiditis.

regimens.label: Non-Antibiotic Options
notes:
- Recommend regular doses of paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, advising maximum, regular doses as appropriate for the child’s weight / age. These products are available to purchase over the counter.

- Consider a prescription for eardrops containing an anaesthetic and an analgesic:

[[green:Phenazone 40 mg/g with lidocaine 10 mg/g: Apply 4 drops two or three times a day for up to 7 days. Use only if an immediate oral antibiotic prescription is not given, and there is no eardrum perforation or otorrhoea.]]
